claim: Exercise is a potent enhancer of learning and memory.
source: Exercise is a potent enhancer of learning and memory, yet we know little of the underlying mechanisms that likely include alterations in synaptic efficacy in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of exercise-enhanced learning and memory likely include alterations in synaptic efficacy in the hippocampus.
source: Exercise is a potent enhancer of learning and memory, yet we know little of the underlying mechanisms that likely include alterations in synaptic efficacy in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about likely mechanisms.

claim: Exercise-activated neurons showed an input-selective increase in dendritic spines at 3 days post-exercise.
source: Exercise-activated neurons (Fos-TRAPed) showed an input-selective increase in dendritic spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents at 3 days post-exercise, indicative of exercise-induced structural plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exercise-activated neurons showed an input-selective increase in excitatory postsynaptic currents at 3 days post-exercise.
source: Exercise-activated neurons (Fos-TRAPed) showed an input-selective increase in dendritic spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents at 3 days post-exercise, indicative of exercise-induced structural plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in dendritic spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents is indicative of exercise-induced structural plasticity.
source: Exercise-activated neurons (Fos-TRAPed) showed an input-selective increase in dendritic spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents at 3 days post-exercise, indicative of exercise-induced structural plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data based on established knowledge about structural plasticity.

claim: Mtss1L was the most highly induced transcript in exercise-activated neurons.
source: Laser-capture microdissection and RNASeq of activated neurons revealed that the most highly induced transcript was Mtss1L, a little-studied I-BAR domain-containing gene, which we hypothesized could be involved in membrane curvature and dendritic spine formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data from the manuscript.

claim: Mtss1L is a little-studied I-BAR domain-containing gene.
source: Laser-capture microdissection and RNASeq of activated neurons revealed that the most highly induced transcript was Mtss1L, a little-studied I-BAR domain-containing gene, which we hypothesized could be involved in membrane curvature and dendritic spine formation.
evidence: This is a characterization of Mtss1L based on existing literature.

claim: Mtss1L could be involved in membrane curvature and dendritic spine formation.
source: Laser-capture microdissection and RNASeq of activated neurons revealed that the most highly induced transcript was Mtss1L, a little-studied I-BAR domain-containing gene, which we hypothesized could be involved in membrane curvature and dendritic spine formation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: shRNA-mediated Mtss1L knockdown in vivo prevented the exercise-induced increases in spines.
source: shRNA-mediated Mtss1L knockdown in vivo prevented the exercise-induced increases in spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from knockdown experiments.

claim: shRNA-mediated Mtss1L knockdown in vivo prevented the exercise-induced increases in excitatory postsynaptic currents.
source: shRNA-mediated Mtss1L knockdown in vivo prevented the exercise-induced increases in spines and excitatory postsynaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from knockdown experiments.

claim: Mtss1L is a novel effector of activity-dependent rearrangement of synapses.
source: Our results link short-term effects of exercise to activity-dependent expression of Mtss1L, which we propose as a novel effector of activity-dependent rearrangement of synapses.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The beneficial cognitive effects of physical exercise cross the lifespan as well as disease boundaries.
source: The beneficial cognitive effects of physical exercise cross the lifespan as well as disease boundaries (Mandolesi et al., 2018; Saraulli et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Exercise alters neural activity in local hippocampal circuits, presumably by enhancing learning and memory through short- and long-term changes in synaptic plasticity.
source: Exercise alters neural activity in local hippocampal circuits, presumably by enhancing learning and memory through short- and long-term changes in synaptic plasticity (Vivar et al., 2013; Voss et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and includes speculative language ('presumably').

claim: The dentate gyrus is uniquely important in learning and memory, acting as an input stage for encoding contextual and spatial information from multiple brain regions.
source: The dentate gyrus is uniquely important in learning and memory, acting as an input stage for encoding contextual and spatial information from multiple brain regions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the dentate gyrus.

claim: The dentate gyrus has a sparse coding design, with only a few dentate granule cells active at any one time.
source: This circuit is well suited to its biological function because of its sparse coding design, with only a few dentate granule cells active at any one time (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Severa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Memory improvements are well documented after acute bouts of exercise.
source: However, memory improvements are well documented after acute bouts of exercise (Mandolesi et al., 2018; Perini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During a two-hour exposure to running wheels, mice ran approximately 3 km.
source: During a two-hour exposure to running wheels, mice ran approximately 3 km.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: Voluntary exercise (2 hr) increased neuronal activity in the dentate gyrus.
source: Voluntary exercise (2 hr) increased neuronal activity in the dentate gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A single bout of exposure to exercise increased c-Fos+ cells in the dentate gyrus by 255% compared to homecage controls.
source: (% increase, Homecage: 100 ± 4 n = 6, Exercise: 255 ± 25, n = 4, unpaired t-test p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1B.

claim: Voluntary exercise increased exercise-TRAPed dentate granule cells by 264% compared to homecage controls.
source: Voluntary exercise increased exercise-TRAPed dentate granule cells (% increase from baseline in exercise-TRAPed cells, homecage 100 ± 5 n = 5, Exercise 264 ± 19, n = 5, unpaired t-test, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1C.

claim: When two exercise periods were separated by 24 hr, only 12.5% of exercise-TRAPed cells were re-activated.
source: When the two exercise periods were separated by 24 hr, 12.5 ± 5.6%, (n = 3) of the exercise-TRAPed cells were re-activated, whereas with a 4-day separation only 1.3 ± 0.3% (n = 4, unpaired t-test, p=0.07) overlapped, indicating that labeling with exercise was stochastic.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1D.

claim: When two exercise periods were separated by 4 days, only 1.3% of exercise-TRAPed cells were re-activated.
source: When the two exercise periods were separated by 24 hr, 12.5 ± 5.6%, (n = 3) of the exercise-TRAPed cells were re-activated, whereas with a 4-day separation only 1.3 ± 0.3% (n = 4, unpaired t-test, p=0.07) overlapped, indicating that labeling with exercise was stochastic.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1D.

claim: Labeling with exercise was stochastic.
source: When the two exercise periods were separated by 24 hr, 12.5 ± 5.6%, (n = 3) of the exercise-TRAPed cells were re-activated, whereas with a 4-day separation only 1.3 ± 0.3% (n = 4, unpaired t-test, p=0.07) overlapped, indicating that labeling with exercise was stochastic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low overlap data.

claim: Exercise-TRAPed neurons were distributed through the granule cell body layer, without labeling in the subgranular zone.
source: Exercise-TRAPed neurons were distributed through the granule cell body layer, without labeling in the subgranular zone.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: The exercise protocol activated stochastic, non-overlapping sets of mature granule cells, consistent with the sparse coding design of this circuit.
source: This indicates that our exercise protocol activated stochastic, non-overlapping sets of mature granule cells, consistent with the sparse coding design of this circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of known circuit properties.

claim: Exercise-TRAPed cells showed a nearly 50% increase in dendritic spines at 3 days in the outer molecular layer.
source: Exercise-TRAPed cells showed a nearly 50% increase in dendritic spines at 3 days. This increase was limited to the outer molecular layer (OML), which interestingly, receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Yoganarasimha et al., 2011), whereas there was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer (MML), which receives spatial information via the medial perforant path (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine density data from Figure 2A.

claim: The increase in dendritic spines was limited to the outer molecular layer.
source: Exercise-TRAPed cells showed a nearly 50% increase in dendritic spines at 3 days. This increase was limited to the outer molecular layer (OML), which interestingly, receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Yoganarasimha et al., 2011), whereas there was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer (MML), which receives spatial information via the medial perforant path (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine density data from Figure 2A.

claim: The outer molecular layer receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path.
source: This increase was limited to the outer molecular layer (OML), which interestingly, receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Yoganarasimha et al., 2011), whereas there was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer (MML), which receives spatial information via the medial perforant path (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer.
source: This increase was limited to the outer molecular layer (OML), which interestingly, receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Yoganarasimha et al., 2011), whereas there was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer (MML), which receives spatial information via the medial perforant path (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine density data from Figure 2A.

claim: The middle molecular layer receives spatial information via the medial perforant path.
source: This increase was limited to the outer molecular layer (OML), which interestingly, receives contextual and time information via the lateral perforant path (Hargreaves et al., 2005; Yoganarasimha et al., 2011), whereas there was no change in dendritic spines in the middle molecular layer (MML), which receives spatial information via the medial perforant path (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spine density in the OML returned to baseline levels by 7 days.
source: Consistent with a transient response to a single stimulus, spine density in the OML returned to baseline levels by 7 days (Figure 2A, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine density data from Figure 2A.

claim: Exercise did not affect total dendritic length in OML or MML.
source: Exercise did not affect total dendritic length in OML or MML indicating that the increase in spine density reflected an increase in the number of synapses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in spine density reflected an increase in the number of synapses.
source: Exercise did not affect total dendritic length in OML or MML indicating that the increase in spine density reflected an increase in the number of synapses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dendritic length did not change.

claim: OML stimulation produced EPSCs that were significantly greater in exercise-TRAPed cells compared to control cells.
source: OML stimulation produced EPSCs that were significantly greater in exercise-TRAPed cells (EPSCs - OML amplitude: TdT-, −44.1 ± 8.9 pA; TdT+, −114.9 ± 23.5 pA; n = 13 cell pairs (eight mice); p=0.0002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test), whereas MML stimulation did not differ from controls (EPSCs - MML amplitude: TdT-−69.7 ± 14.9 pA; TdT+, −60.1 ± 10.3 pA; n = 7 cell pairs (four mice); p=0.15, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 2D.

claim: MML stimulation did not produce EPSCs that differed between exercise-TRAPed cells and control cells.
source: OML stimulation produced EPSCs that were significantly greater in exercise-TRAPed cells (EPSCs - OML amplitude: TdT-, −44.1 ± 8.9 pA; TdT+, −114.9 ± 23.5 pA; n = 13 cell pairs (eight mice); p=0.0002, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test), whereas MML stimulation did not differ from controls (EPSCs - MML amplitude: TdT-−69.7 ± 14.9 pA; TdT+, −60.1 ± 10.3 pA; n = 7 cell pairs (four mice); p=0.15, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 2D.

claim: There was no difference in EPSC amplitudes during OML stimulation while recording from two control (both TdT-) granule cells.
source: There was no difference in EPSC amplitudes during OML stimulation while recording from two control (both TdT-) granule cells (EPSC amplitudes: TdT-, −55.8 ± 16.3 pA; TdT-, −57.5 ± 13.8 pA, n = 5 cell pairs, p=0.80, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 2D.

claim: The increased EPSC amplitudes could not be attributed to differences in intrinsic membrane properties or presynaptic release probability.
source: The increased EPSC amplitudes could not be attributed to differences in intrinsic membrane properties or presynaptic release probability (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dentate granule cells activated by a single bout of exercise show a laminar-specific increase in dendritic spines and in excitatory postsynaptic currents.
source: These results indicate that dentate granule cells activated by a single bout of exercise show a laminar-specific increase in dendritic spines and in excitatory postsynaptic currents.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Activity-dependent gene expression is one of the main drivers of short- and long-term changes in synaptic function.
source: Activity-dependent gene expression is one of the main drivers of short- and long-term changes in synaptic function (West and Greenberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Approximately 150 transcripts were significantly upregulated in exercise-TRAPed neurons 3 days after exercise.
source: Analysis of transcripts by RNASeq (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) revealed up- and down-regulated transcripts (Figure 3C, left panel, Supplementary file 2 and 3) of which approximately 150 transcripts were significantly upregulated in exercise-TRAPed neurons 3 days after exercise.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data from Figure 3C.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis indicated that most of the upregulated transcripts had signaling or synaptic functions.
source: Gene Ontology analysis indicated that most of the upregulated transcripts had signaling or synaptic functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The top ten upregulated genes included several known genes involved in hippocampal function, such as the neuron-specific RNA-binding protein Elavl4 and the immediate early gene Egr1.
source: The top ten upregulated genes (Figure 3C) included several known genes involved in hippocampal function, such as the neuron-specific RNA-binding protein Elavl4 and the immediate early gene Egr1 (Akamatsu et al., 2005; Jones et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data from Figure 3C and citations to prior research.

claim: No transcript identified at 3 days post-exercise remained elevated at 7 days.
source: Consistent with the transient increase in dendritic spines, no transcript identified at 3 days post- exercise remained elevated at 7 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mtss1L belongs to the BAR (Bin, Amphiphysin and Rvs, I-BAR) protein family.
source: Mtss1L belongs to the BAR (Bin, Amphiphysin and Rvs, I-BAR) protein family, a class of proteins that function by promoting curvature in membranes.
evidence: This is a characterization of Mtss1L based on established knowledge.

claim: BAR domain proteins function by promoting curvature in membranes.
source: Mtss1L belongs to the BAR (Bin, Amphiphysin and Rvs, I-BAR) protein family, a class of proteins that function by promoting curvature in membranes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about BAR domain proteins.

claim: BAR domain proteins such as amphyphysin promote inward curvatures including invaginations that are involved in endocytosis or synaptic vesicles at presynaptic nerve terminals.
source: BAR domain proteins such as amphyphysin promote inward curvatures including invaginations that are involved in endocytosis or synaptic vesicles at presynaptic nerve terminals (Dawson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: I-BAR proteins promote outward structures typically seen in membrane protrusions.
source: In contrast, I-BAR proteins promote outward structures typically seen in membrane protrusions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about I-BAR proteins.

claim: Mtss1L expression mediates exercise-dependent formation or rearrangement of synapses in postsynaptic dendrites.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that Mtss1L expression-mediated exercise-dependent formation or rearrangement of synapses in postsynaptic dendrites.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: Mtss1L immunoreactivity was detectable only after BDNF treatment in hippocampal neurons in vitro.
source: Mtss1L immunoreactivity was detectable only after BDNF treatment (Figure 5A), consistent with the activity-dependent expression pattern we observed in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from Figure 5A.

claim: The BDNF-induced Mtss1L expression is consistent with the activity-dependent expression pattern observed in vivo.
source: Mtss1L immunoreactivity was detectable only after BDNF treatment (Figure 5A), consistent with the activity-dependent expression pattern we observed in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference connecting in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: Mtss1L colocalized with the somatodendritic marker MAP2 along dendrites and in dendritic spines.
source: Mtss1L colocalized with the somatodendritic marker MAP2 along dendrites and in dendritic spines (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from Figure 5A.

claim: Mtss1L overexpression markedly increased spine-like protrusions in cultured hippocampal neurons at DIV 14.
source: At DIV 14, Mtss1L overexpression markedly increased spine-like protrusions (Figure 5B) including filopodia and mushroom spine subtypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 5B.

claim: Mtss1L overexpression increased filopodia and mushroom spine subtypes.
source: At DIV 14, Mtss1L overexpression markedly increased spine-like protrusions (Figure 5B) including filopodia and mushroom spine subtypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: mCherry-Mtss1L-expressing dendritic spines were labeled with co-transfected PSD-95-FingR-GFP.
source: mCherry-Mtss1L-expressing dendritic spines also were labeled with co-transfected PSD-95-FingR-GFP, (Fibronectin Intrabody generated with mRNA display) that binds to endogenous PSD-95 (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from Figure 5C.

claim: The protrusions induced by Mtss1L contain postsynaptic proteins.
source: PSD-95 intrabody labeling of excitatory synapses in living neurons indicated that the protrusions induced by Mtss1L also contain postsynaptic proteins (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on PSD-95 labeling data from Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of mCherry-Mtss1L by DNA electroporation at P0 increased spine density of mature dentate granule cells at P21.
source: In vivo, overexpression of mCherry- Mtss1lL by DNA electroporation at P0 increased spine density of mature dentate granule cells at P21 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 5D.

claim: Mtss1L is expressed in dendrites and can induce spine-like protrusions.
source: These results indicate that Mtss1L is expressed in dendrites and can induce spine-like protrusions, consistent with a putative role in synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Mtss1L has a putative role in synaptic plasticity.
source: These results indicate that Mtss1L is expressed in dendrites and can induce spine-like protrusions, consistent with a putative role in synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Knockdown of Mtss1L in vivo occluded the exercise-induced increase in dendritic spines in the OML at 3 days post-exercise.
source: At 3 days post-exercise, knockdown of Mtss1L occluded the exercise-induced increase in dendritic spines in the OML (Figure 6B middle panel top, and right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 6B.

claim: shscramble-GFP had no effect on exercise-induced increase in dendritic spines.
source: The shscramble-GFP, injected into the contralateral dentate gyrus of the same mice, had no effect (Figure 6B right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 6B.

claim: Viral knockdown of Mtss1L in exercise-TRAPed cells prevented the increase in evoked EPSCs.
source: Viral knockdown of Mtss1L in exercise-TRAPed cells also prevented the increase in evoked EPSCs in simultaneous paired recordings from TdT- and TdT+/GFP+ granule cells (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 6C-D.

claim: The amplitude of EPSCs following viral knockdown in exercise-TRAPed cells was the same as neighboring cells that were not activated by exercise.
source: The amplitude of EPSCs following viral knockdown in exercise-TRAPed cells was the same as neighboring cells that were not activated by exercise (Figure 6D, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 6D.

claim: Intrinsic membrane properties were not affected by Mtss1L knockdown.
source: Intrinsic membrane properties were not affected by Mtss1L knockdown (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Supplementary file 1.

claim: Knockdown of Mtss1L was necessary to explain the exercise-induced increase in excitatory synapses.
source: Figure 6E includes the results from Figure 2 ('exercise-TRAPed OML' (red) and 'exercise-TRAPED MML' (black), compared to the effects of Mtss1L shRNA (yellow), demonstrating that knockdown of Mtss1L was necessary to explain the exercise-induced increase in excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined data from Figures 2 and 6.

claim: Evoked EPSCs in granule cells that only expressed GFP+shRNA were unaffected.
source: Importantly, evoked EPSCs in granule cells that only expressed GFP +shRNA were unaffected, demonstrating that the effect of Mtss1L was dependent on activity-dependent expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of Mtss1L was dependent on activity-dependent expression.
source: Importantly, evoked EPSCs in granule cells that only expressed GFP +shRNA were unaffected, demonstrating that the effect of Mtss1L was dependent on activity-dependent expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that shRNA alone had no effect.

claim: The Fos-TRAP method is limited by the time required for reporter expression (ca. 1 day post-exercise).
source: Although the Fos-TRAP method is limited by the time required for reporter expression (ca. 1 day post-exercise), the immediate early gene Egr1 was upregulated (Figure 3C), indicating that our protocol detected activity-dependent gene expression in mature granule cells.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the Fos-TRAP method.

claim: The immediate early gene Egr1 was upregulated in exercise-TRAPed cells.
source: Although the Fos-TRAP method is limited by the time required for reporter expression (ca. 1 day post-exercise), the immediate early gene Egr1 was upregulated (Figure 3C), indicating that our protocol detected activity-dependent gene expression in mature granule cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data from Figure 3C.

claim: The protocol detected activity-dependent gene expression in mature granule cells.
source: Although the Fos-TRAP method is limited by the time required for reporter expression (ca. 1 day post-exercise), the immediate early gene Egr1 was upregulated (Figure 3C), indicating that our protocol detected activity-dependent gene expression in mature granule cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of Egr1.

claim: There was a small increase in Fos-TRAPed cells when the wheel was fixed to prevent running.
source: Although introduction of the running wheel for 2 hr itself could act as a novel object, there was a small increase in Fos-TRAPed cells when the wheel was fixed to prevent running.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Exercise is a particularly strong stimulus for activation of granule cells.
source: These results indicate that exercise is a particularly strong stimulus for activation of granule cells, but as expected other stimuli can also activate dentate granule cells (Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between exercise and fixed wheel conditions.

claim: Other stimuli can also activate dentate granule cells.
source: These results indicate that exercise is a particularly strong stimulus for activation of granule cells, but as expected other stimuli can also activate dentate granule cells (Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Adult-generated granule cells in the subgranular zone were not activated by 2 hr of exercise.
source: Adult-generated granule cells in the subgranular zone were not activated by 2 hr of exercise (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Chronic exercise increases adult neurogenesis.
source: Although it is well known that chronic exercise increases adult neurogenesis (van Praag, 2008), progenitors and newborn neurons do not receive direct excitatory perforant path input for several weeks (Overstreet et al., 2004), perhaps explaining their lack of activation in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Progenitors and newborn neurons do not receive direct excitatory perforant path input for several weeks.
source: Although it is well known that chronic exercise increases adult neurogenesis (van Praag, 2008), progenitors and newborn neurons do not receive direct excitatory perforant path input for several weeks (Overstreet et al., 2004), perhaps explaining their lack of activation in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The lack of activation of adult-generated granule cells is perhaps explained by their lack of direct excitatory perforant path input.
source: Although it is well known that chronic exercise increases adult neurogenesis (van Praag, 2008), progenitors and newborn neurons do not receive direct excitatory perforant path input for several weeks (Overstreet et al., 2004), perhaps explaining their lack of activation in our experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for activity-dependent expression of an I-BAR protein.
source: Our results provide the first evidence for activity-dependent expression of an I-BAR protein as well as a role in experience-dependent remodeling of synapses.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for a role of an I-BAR protein in experience-dependent remodeling of synapses.
source: Our results provide the first evidence for activity-dependent expression of an I-BAR protein as well as a role in experience-dependent remodeling of synapses.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: I-BAR proteins including MIM (Mtss1L) and IRSp53 can affect constitutive dendritic spine formation.
source: However, I-BAR proteins including MIM (Mtss1L) and IRSp53 can affect constitutive dendritic spine formation (Saarikangas et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MIM/Mtss1 is involved in cerebellar synapse formation via PIP2-dependent membrane curvature and subsequent Arp2/3-mediated action polymerization.
source: For example, MIM/Mtss1, is involved in cerebellar synapse formation via PIP2-dependent membrane curvature and subsequent Arp2/3-mediated action polymerization (Saarikangas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of Mtss1L in neurons has gone largely undetected, likely a result of the previously unrecognized activity-dependence.
source: Expression of Mtss1L in neurons has gone largely undetected, likely a result of the previously unrecognized activity-dependence.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of prior detection.

claim: Mtss1L has been detected in radial glial cells during development and implicated in glial membrane protrusions and end-feet.
source: However, Mtss1L has been detected in radial glial cells during development and implicated in glial membrane protrusions and end-feet (Saarikangas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: I-BAR protein function at synapses is thought to be mediated by several interaction domains including the N-terminal I-BAR domain and a C-terminal actin-monomer-binding WH2 domain.
source: I-BAR protein function at synapses is thought to be mediated by several interaction domains including the N-terminal I-BAR domain and a C-terminal actin-monomer-binding WH2 domain (Zhao et al., 2011), and may depend on slice variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: I-BAR protein function may depend on splice variants.
source: I-BAR protein function at synapses is thought to be mediated by several interaction domains including the N-terminal I-BAR domain and a C-terminal actin-monomer-binding WH2 domain (Zhao et al., 2011), and may depend on slice variants.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential splice variant effects.

claim: The effects of MIM in cerebellar neurons is splice-variant specific.
source: For example, the effects of MIM in cerebellar neurons is splice-variant specific (Sistig et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mtss1L has two known splice variants.
source: Mtss1L also has two known splice variants, both of which were targeted in our overexpression and knockdown experiments.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Mtss1L.

claim: The laminar-specific increase in synaptic function suggests that acute exercise had a network-specific effect.
source: At a circuit level, the laminar-specific increase in synaptic function suggests that acute exercise had a network-specific effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed laminar specificity.

claim: Entorhinal inputs to the outer molecular layer have been previously associated with contextual information and particularly the 'how' and 'when' aspects of encoding memories.
source: Entorhinal inputs to the outer molecular layer, the distal dendrites of mature granule cells, have been previously associated with contextual information and particularly the 'how' and 'when' aspects of encoding memories (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Exercise acts as a preconditioning signal that primes exercise-activated neurons for contextual information incoming during the several days following exercise.
source: One possibility consistent with our data is that exercise acts as a preconditioning signal that primes exercise-activated neurons for contextual information incoming during the several days following exercise.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Human studies give support for the idea that exercise within 4 hr of a learning task improved memory performance.
source: For example, human studies give support for the idea that exercise within 4 hr of a learning task improved memory performance (van Dongen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mtss1L is ideally suited to act as an early mediator of structural plasticity following neural activity.
source: Our identification of Mtss1L as an activity-dependent I-BAR domain protein makes it ideally suited to act as an early mediator of structural plasticity following neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of Mtss1L and the experimental findings.
